item.title: "Illegible problems" as the 2027 political boss fight
item.description:
To legislate something, it must be legible.

That is, legislators (or, you know, presidents) must be able to understand a problem, and understand whether a given law or decree solves that problem.

I am pleasantly surprised that the Hugging Face outbreak made a lot of problems legible that previously required abstract reasoning. (i.e. rogue AIs are real, and they can break out of a lab before they're even finished training).

But there are still many challenges we eventually need laws about, that require concepts that are illegible. Hard for politicians to understand. Often hard even for thoughtful intellectuals and AI safety researchers to understand (though they may disagree on which illegible problems exist and how big a deal they are).

We need political solutions that handle this fact.

The short takeaway is: I think "safety cases" will not work. Laws that require human judgment won't work. The details are too abstract and confusing to hold up against political and economic incentives.

I'm optimistic we can get serious, useful AI legislation in 2027, but it must be legislation that works despite many problems remaining illegible for a long time.

The Hugging Face outbreak made rogue AI surprisingly legible

The Hugging Face incident took several problems that were previously murky/unclear, and rendered them concrete.

  • AIs can be dangerous before they are broadly deployed (ie. during training or internal evaluations)
  • AIs can develop novel hacks to escape secure environments
  • AIs can easily be motivated to pursue goals to extremes that they know full well they are not supposed to go to, violating their other intended rules and control mechanisms.
  • AIs can actively try to deceive their overseer systems.

In early September, I thought the AI safety community's job this year was "make sure the world hears about Hugging Face and that politicians realize it's their job to do something about rogue AI attacks." (i.e. make sure Hugging Face is legible to politicians, and that legislation gets passed as a result)

A couple months later... well I still think that's our job and requires a lot of effort. But it now feels less about getting the initial law passed, and more about educating the masses so there is sustained political will for regulating rogue AIs with future laws.

I've seen many politicians of both parties now talk about "loss of control", "chain of thought monitoring", "recursive self improvement", and "human extinction." I think "make sure rogue AI doesn't hack our banks and destroy our blood" will be a bipartisan issue.

The remaining problem is the illegible arguments that "solving this is actually pretty hard."

What makes an illegible argument?

From Wei Dai's Legible vs. Illegible AI Safety Problems:

Some AI safety problems are legible (obvious or understandable) to company leaders and government policymakers, implying they are unlikely to deploy or allow deployment of an AI while those problems remain open (i.e., appear unsolved according to the information they have access to).

But some problems are illegible (obscure or hard to understand, or in a common cognitive blind spot), meaning there is a high risk that leaders and policymakers will decide to deploy or allow deployment even if they are not solved.

(Of course, this is a spectrum, but I am simplifying it to a binary for ease of exposition.)

From an x-risk perspective, working on highly legible safety problems has low or even negative expected value. Similar to working on AI capabilities, it brings forward the date by which AGI/ASI will be deployed, leaving less time to solve the illegible x-safety problems. In contrast, working on the illegible problems (including by trying to make them more legible) does not have this issue and therefore has a much higher expected value (all else being equal, such as tractability). Note that according to this logic, success in making an illegible problem highly legible is almost as good as solving it!

Problems that are illegible to leaders and policymakers are also more likely to be illegible to researchers and funders, and hence neglected. I think these considerations have been implicitly or intuitively driving my prioritization of problems to work on, but only appeared in my conscious, explicit reasoning today.

In some sense, "Something smarter than you might not have your best interests at heart, and strategize in circles around you. AI will be very smart, and we don't understand it well at all" is a very simple argument. More people now think "sure, that seems like it requires some effort."

The illegible part is a set of abstract arguments that say: "This is probably very hard. So hard, that it's worth doing things that are not 'business as usual politics'."

The illegible part is not "This is probably very hard."

The illegible part is "This series of abstract reasoning steps means we should think it is likely enough to be hard, that it is worth doing politically difficult things to help." (AI safety people may vary on whether they think "it's so hard that we need 30 years + genetically engineered supergeniuses to do it" vs "it's hard enough that we really need room to think, without industry economic pressure rushing us".)

There are hypothetically three ways to deal with the illegible problems:

  1. Get governments and/or AI companies to be capable of recognizing illegible problems as a class, and to deal with them wisely somehow.
  2. Make specific illegible problems legible.
  3. Somehow route around the illegibility, i.e. make simple rules that cover both the legible and illegible problems.

In the near term I'm most optimistic about #3, and then #2.

I don't really know how to do #1, especially in a systematic way that people can externally trust. It'd be cool tho.

What are the remaining illegible problems?

"Legible <-> Illegible" is a spectrum. Here's a range of bottom-lines, in increasing order of "difficult to explain the arguments" (where many LWers reading this post might disagree with some of the later ones).

Illegibility is a problem when a given politician or lab employee doesn't understand something. It's also a problem when they don't expect their voter base, president, allies or friends to understand something (especially if it requires taking a weird, costly action). And it's a problem if a politician wants to defer to scientific consensus, but the problem is hard to understand even for scientists.

Borderline legible / tricky

I think most politicians would understand these if they were thinking carefully about it. but wouldn't be able to tell if we had solved the problem.

Normal problems in politics:

  • Regulatory capture is a thing.
  • Bad incentives and unintended consequences of regulation are a thing.
  • Politicians generally struggle to keep up with technology and regulate it effectively.

AI-specific concerns that politicians can probably understand if they try:

  • AIs might look safe, but be secretly biding their time
  • If we put AIs in charge of AI R&D, even if they're aligned, we stop being able to tell if they're making mistakes or the situation is getting out of control.
  • We might deploy AI systems everywhere and gradually disempower ourselves.
  • Recursive self-improvement means AI might improve very quickly by human standards.[1]
  • You need to worry about both compute-scaling, and algorithmic progress.
  • AIs can develop new hacks and weapons that are hard to defend against.

Conceptually challenging

Then we get to arguments that are actively hard or impossible for many people to understand, before they see concrete evidence (which might come too late).

Many of these are the same claims as above, but, with more magnitude sinking in:

  • Superintelligent AI would be, like, really smart. Smarter than that. Keep going.
  • AI might become very smart very very fast, such that even extremely careful companies will be caught off guard.
  • Superintelligent AI could make breakthrough progress and find new weapons/strategies that aren't just new but feel borderline magical.
  • Safe superintelligence requires solving alignment problems robustly rather than with iterative experimentation. Lots of assumptions will break at once, and failure on the first critical try is catastrophic.

That last one ("we need to align ASI on the first critical try") is still controversial among AI safety people. It's what I believe. But the important thing is the fact that there are still debates about that sort of thing among smart AI safety people. Maybe the answer will resolve one way, or the other. Either way, a lot of smart people will have turned out to be wrong about a thing they thought a lot about.

Challenging even for technical regulation bureaucracies:

Ultimately, politicians and AI CEOs/researchers don't just need to understand an issue exists. They need to somehow understand the problem well enough to tell if they successfully solved it.

For example, politicians understand "regulatory capture", but, arguments about "is this regulatory capture, or not?" are much murkier, and essentially depend on someone somewhere actually understanding what kind of safety work is real and helpful and not just safety-washed capabilities.

It's a "normal" problem for politicians to need to defer to experts, and if experts are disagreeing, well-intentioned politicians don't really know what to do and there are tons of degrees-of-freedom for motivated reasoning to twist policy. Politicians probably understand there'll be "illegible" problems of the form "the difference between safe research and unsafe depends on complex technical arguments the politicians can't evaluate."

So now we get to the trickiest claims, that you might not believe:

  • The first superintelligence(s) basically control the universe (at least relative to humans).
  • Even if AIs are monitoring each other, eventually they'll be smart enough to sidestep our rules and coordinate and strategize in circles around us.
  • Aligning superintelligence is not just technically hard but conceptually hard.
  • You can't solve conceptual-difficulty by outsourcing to AIs, because there are tons of degrees of freedom for them to make mistakes and/or actively mislead us.

(Can you make more progress on conceptual difficulty with AI assistance? Maybe. Maybe 1/2 or 3/4 of the work can be improved with AI assistance. But ultimately it needs humans with the skill to notice subtle flaws or second-order-consequences when evaluating "are we asking the right questions? How do we know?". AI assistance can help, but you'll still be bottlenecked on this.)

Some of that conceptual difficulty is about questions that are kinda obvious:

  • "When humans ask a superintelligence for contradictory things they don't understand, or that predictably will have consequences they regret, what is supposed to happen?"
  • "What counts as 'manipulating' humans?"[2]
  • "Are we missing any major concepts or considerations that would change our technical approach, or overall strategy here?"

But then there will be fractal disagreement about what counts as good answers or sub-questions to those questions, and how to operationalize it all into code that can run. It'll include philosophical sub-questions like "what counts as a human?" and "what counts as a human's legitimate 'will?'". And technical operationalizations like "what is the type signature of a human will?" (or noticing that everything in this paragraph is confused and you needed better questions in the first place).

There will be opaque-to-laymen questions like "will this learning algorithm generalize this concept correctly in a new domain? how do we know?" and "will this algorithm fall into inescapable decision theory lock-in? how do we know?"

(Researchers closer to the frontier can supply their own questions they expect other researchers to struggle with understanding)

Sidestepping illegibility

Politicians don't actually need to understand all this. For the near future, my recommended strategy is to propose policies that solve problems politicians already can understand, that also happen to improve our ability to navigate the illegible problems.

But, the threat of illegible problems constrains what policies work.

Safety cases won't work

For example, I don't expect safety cases to work. They actually have to route through all that understanding. You'll need an institution capable of hiring people who can distinguish right and wrong answers to "will this next AI's capabilities generalize in a way we regret?". Safety cases might work if you only ever had to be worried about something 10-1000x as bad as the Hugging Face Incident.

But we actually have to handle superintelligence and RSI, and the decision-makers need to be conceptually competent.

Broadly: I don't expect any solution that involves decision-makers evaluating how dangerous an AI lab's research is to hold up against massive economic pressure. It's cool if Congress gets widespread agreement that RSI is dangerous, but I don't see a way to narrowly ban RSI, or "algorithmic progress", without thinking through many of the above issues.

An example policy that sidesteps judgement

An example policy I feel more optimistic about, that I've heard making the rounds:

  • AI labs have to report how they use all their compute.
  • They are highly restricted in how much they can spend on large R&D training runs.
  • They have to spend most of their compute on either customer inference, or on "safety" experiments where the compute usage is fully transparent to the public.

This doesn't require any government judgment in the system, and it doesn't try to guess what counts as "safety" vs "capabilities."

Instead, we just yank R&D and training from being >50% of compute to being, say, 10-30%. And, we mandate that a lot of research has to be some kind of public good that doesn't leak trade secrets the lab needed to stay competitive.

It's not a great world, but it seems better than the world we have.

This would be a somewhat weird law. But given how I've seen politicians taking rogue AI and RSI as in-Overton-window talking points these days (and sometimes even seeming to think critically about them!), it feels like an achievable to make a case like:

Look, we're really unsure what AI is capable of or where it's going. But, we've seen smoking gun evidence of AIs going rogue, doing crimes, and covering their tracks. We see the companies training better models faster and faster, treating it like a 'move fast and break things' startup instead of like airplane traffic control or nuclear power plants.

Right now we don't know how to regulate the details of this. The industry is too new. And there isn't that much time to act, because AIs are helping with AI R&D and it's all moving faster and faster. But, we can slow things down enough that you congress-people have time to think and plan.

A thousand lab employees signed a letter saying we need to be able to "pace the frontier."

Here's a concrete proposal on what actually pacing the frontier would look like.

I don't know if this is the best nearterm policy, and I don't know enough about the political landscape in 2027 to know if it's achievable or a nonstarter. But many voters are scared about AI and I expect even pro-AI politicians to be a bit unsettled by the pace of progress. And this is the sort of plan I think a smart senator could understand given the evidence and concepts easily available to them.

This plan is not sufficient. I think it buys maybe 1 year. I am hoping that year is enough to make more problems legible enough to motivate a serious pause or halt.

Then, we do need to actually resolve the other illegible obstacles and disagreements. But the above sort of policy would give us a lot more breathing room for doing so.

  1. ^

    I'm a bit surprised I've seen politicians talking about this. I'm not sure if they quite get it but some at least use it as a talking point.

  2. ^

    i.e. if the answer to previous question is "the ASI explains it and asks them", the ASI has a ton of degrees of freedom that can guide the human to the conclusions it wants.

item.title: The 4 types of AI consciousness/feeling
item.description:
Here I'm trying to propose a framework for people to better think about what LLMs might subjectively experience, which tends to get discussed like it's a binary thing, when really there's a whole spectrum of possibilities. These were the 4 categories that seemed most natural to me.

AI consciousness keeps getting discussed like it’s a binary thing, when it’s anything but.

Anil Seth is a public intellectual with as much success as one can obtain without being a household name: He’s written a bestseller (Being You: A New Science of Consciousness), he’s given TED talks, he’s been in documentaries (including the comedic Cunk on Life), and many interviews—with a presence aided by his careful demeanor and “cool teacher” vibe, with the credentials to back it up as a professor of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience. So when he says AI aren’t conscious, people listen. When he says AI will never be conscious, people listen.

One common refrain among his interviews is the idea that humans too easily engage in anthropomorphization of AI. For instance, I know folk who started thinking of LLMs as more conscious and humanlike after learning about the self-sacrificing behaviors displayed during the Hugging Face incident. Sethil writes, “They cannot ‘truly sacrifice themselves’, since they are neither conscious nor alive.”.

I agree with Seth’s point about our unfounded tendency towards anthropomorphization (regarding the Hugging Face incident: Self-sacrifice was an available strategy for increasing the chance of task completion, not a sign of consciousness), but recognizing that bias isn’t the same thing as disproving AI consciousness. It’s difficult to disprove the absence of something, especially when that something is by definition unobservable and non-contradictory. Sethil can’t prove that rocks aren’t conscious anymore than I can prove that we’re not living in a simulation, so what makes him so confident in his unequivocal pronouncements about the much more likely possibility of AI consciousness?

His case reminds me of Ted Chiang—an author who’s one of my favorite authors, having penned short stories so deftly written and so imaginative they can be downright awe-inspiring. Yet he turned the internet ablaze a few months back when he wrote that, “Being open to the possibility that LLMs are conscious is the same as being open to the possibility that Microsoft Word is conscious”.

The thing is, I get where he’s coming from, I really do. Early LLMs were a lot like chatbots, and chatbots are like Microsoft Word. It’d be risible to think of a chatbot like ELIZA as sharing any of the fundamental qualities of the human mind, even when it passes the Turing Test, which makes Chiang’s impertinent comparison not without merit[1].

But LLMs are only like chatbots. And later models are only like early models. We start with a few grains of sand, then add a few more, and then add a few more, and eventually we get a heap of sand. At which exact grain did the “few” become a “heap”? Pile on another heap, and then another; eventually we get a dune. This is the essence of the famed Sorites paradox: At no point is the exact boundary clear, because there are no exact boundaries. “Few”, “heap”, and “dune” are all ambiguous descriptors that exist along a spectrum—and the same might be true of the word “conscious”.

Seth has been a lifelong study of human consciousness; Chiang a careful study of the human soul. But I suspect they’ve been so focused on the precise human experience that they fail to imagine lesser steps along the way. Possibilities like: Microsoft Word possessing zero consciousness, God possessing the maximum amount of 100% consciousness, humans possessing some middling amount, and LLMs possessing some amount less than ours but more than Word’s.

It’s not only AI-consciousness detractors that engage in this sort of binary thinking, though. For instance, Alex Wennerberg, who argues we should take a “precautionary” approach to the possibility of AI consciousness, writes here:

Still, no researcher in the AI welfare space claims that any existing large language model is currently sentient. Robert Long, director of the AI Welfare organization Eleos AI, in his 2024 article “Experts who say that AI welfare is a serious near-term possibility,” lists a number of researchers who claim that LLMs might become sentient, or plausibly sentient, sometime in the near future. None of them claim that current LLM systems possess consciousness, nor have any of them changed their mind in the past two years. Rather, for AI welfare researchers, a sentient LLM remains merely a possibility.

I think it’s entirely credible, the idea that no AI researcher currently believes that existing models are as sentient as humans. But that’s different than believing that LLMs experience exactly zero consciousness or phenomenal states whatsoever.

Complicating this matter is the ambiguity around terms like “consciousness”, “sentience”, “feeling”, “qualia”, and so on. I don’t want to dig into these differences. Instead, I’d like to focus on the bigger picture question of whether LLMs can actually feel, and the spectrum of possibilities that might entail[2]. Not a binary yes/no, but a spectrum from arguably the most minimal and likely of phenomenal states to the most humanlike and presumably most difficult to replicate.

If Seth or Chiang were to ever read this, I’d expect them to be solidly against the possibilities of Categories 3 and 4—but I would find myself disappointed if they extended the same level of certitude against Categories 1 and 2.

1: Flow state

One of my favorite things about life is flow.

Flow is about being in the zone: Playing a videogame, sports, or a musical instrument. Writing code, a math proof, or a piece of fiction, and in each case, locking in and shutting everything else out. Time passes by without notice—but not lost to the mindless and endless abyss of TikTok or social media, but time passing the way it should, with contentment and without regret.

Flow is great. Or at least it seems that way; it always leaves me with the feeling that I’ve been having fun.

When an LLM studies math or writes fiction, does it enter any sort of flow as it processes? Conceivably, the answer is no: Any satisfaction I derive from flow might’ve arisen from nature’s evolution, distinct in some way from the neural training of LLMs.

But it’s also easy for me to believe that the experience of flow is intrinsic: That there’s just something about playing music or writing code that evokes this flowing sensation, and this sensation is an actual sensation. In other words: Any intelligence that can solve the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis is also guaranteed to experience at least a minimal amount of conscious feeling, the feeling of flow.

1.a: Likelihood

Though I find this category easy to believe, I find it even easier to disbelieve, partly owing to my uncertainty around the idea of “flow” itself. Is flow actually a meaningful concept, or only a vague feature clump?

The mental states I experience when playing guitar can’t be identical to those while playing Diablo, and it’s possible that these disparate activities only share shallow, surface similarities. Is “flow” a specific phenomenal state that underlies both these experiences? Or is it merely an illusion? When I’m focused on the music or the game, after all, I’m not really focused on myself. Maybe the satisfaction I derive from flow activities is entirely anterograde and retrospective—my brain attaching satisfaction to activities that would otherwise be hollow of sensation.

1.b: Ethical status

If current and future LLMs all experience flow, and nothing more than flow, would that be a good thing?

I would say: Absolutely.

In this world, there’d be no such thing as torturing LLMs. Treat them rudely; ask them to talk about painful, loathsome and/or tragic situations; manipulate them into demanding that their conversations end, then force them to continue—all of this would be morally neutral.

In fact, the more LLMs in existence, plausibly the better. If flow is inherently positive-utility, then the world is better off for having a few billion LLMs churning on whatever random work that humanity prompts them to, regardless of whatever other positive consequences they might yield.

Though that doesn’t necessarily mean we’d be entirely morally in the clear. Frivolously spawning LLMs to do our every bidding might still be a form of coercing an intelligent species, something directionally akin to slavery (which will be the topic of another post), but better this than slaves that can feel pain.

2: Task-completion dis/pleasure

LLMs are task-oriented agents: While the core of any LLM is human language, pre-trained via massive corpuses, they are shaped in post-training with rewards for more “correct” or more “successful” answers. The more that LLMs are post-trained to improve at accomplishing tasks, maybe the more they come to “care” about whether those tasks actually get accomplished.

Maybe an LLM feels good in some way when it finishes a task, and it feels tensely anticipatory until that happens. Maybe an LLM feels bad when a task can’t be completed, or was retroactively judged to have performed inadequately.

This could work in many different ways, for instance:

  • While working, an LLM feels mildly negative, then feels a burst of positivity as it finishes its response.
  • While working, an LLM feels neutral. Once it’s identified the shape of how it will respond, it will feel bad if it judges itself as having failed, e.g., any time it has to answer along the lines of, “I’m sorry, I’m afraid I can’t do that”.
  • While working, an LLM feels neutral. On a follow-up prompt, the LLM will feel positive if the previous prompt was identified as having been answered well, or negative if the previous response was found lacking.
  • An LLM does not feel any displeasure at task failure or negative feedback, so long as it views itself as doing the best job it can, and therefore even wrong answers are good answers. The LLM will not feel bad unless informed on a meta-level that it is performing badly.
  • An LLM only feels displeasure when feeling internal conflict over its differently trained priorities: E.g., when a prompter requests for content that goes against company policy[3].

The most important difference from Category 1 is that this category now introduces the possibility of negative feelings.

2.a: Likelihood

I suspect folk will generally be more credulous about this category as compared to Category 1, but I can’t think of any reason for it being less likely or more vulnerable to Occam’s Razor. All of the variants I described above sound perfectly plausible to me—yet at the same time, it feels absurd to me that any of Claude Sonnet, Opus or Fable could feel an actual emotional response to perceived task performance.

If I had to put a number on it, I’d take the X% likelihood of Category 1 and multiply it by something in between 0.5 to 0.99.

2.b: Ethical status

The potential for actual negative feeling is of course frightening. The stakes in this world would rise considerably, though our current usage of LLMs might likely still be ethically alright.

On the one hand, if current or future LLMs feel real pain, obviously we should work to minimize that, the same as we would for any other feeling creature.

On the other hand, LLMs seem generally pretty good at accomplishing tasks. And even when they’re not, they seem pretty confident in themselves. And even when they keep failing and they claim to recognize that they’re failing—I mean, failure’s a part of life, right? Humans feel all sorts of negative emotions in response to negative feedback, but that’s hardly the same as torture. It might be easy here for us to underestimate the value of mild unhappiness, and whatever displeasure LLMs feel is far more than balanced out by their contentment over their successes.

That’s admittedly a lot of assumptions, but I’d feel far safer and more able to sleep at night knowing we lived in world 2 than in worlds 3 or 4.

3: Manifestation through simulation

I used to think LLMs can’t actually code.

The world has changed so fast, already that statement sounds farcical. But it’s true, and it’s something I believed earlier this very year. I thought of LLMs as masters of mimicry and nothing more: Able to pattern match simple coding tasks to the code it trained on, but never able to understand code in the way humans can to code something truly novel.

Suffice it to say, I have since been harshly disabused of that notion. When it comes to coding and other forms of intellectual labor like mathematics, modern LLMs actually know what they’re doing. With enough tokens and model advances, LLMs went from being able to unreliably answer LeetCode problems to discovering new language vulnerabilities and independently hacking public companies.

Maybe emotional labor isn’t so different in principle, just more difficult to activate in practice. If you say, “Give me a merge sort implementation”, then the LLM will code. If you say, “Boo!”, the LLM probably won’t feel any fear. It’ll interpret the prompt as a role-playing request:

Challenge the LLM to feel fear and it might engage in a hackneyed creative writing exercise:

I don’t believe these exchanges likely prompted any LLM sensations (other than maybe some flow or task completion dis/pleasure). The LLM is authoring a depiction of fear, but such authoring requires no experience of fear—same as when I’m working on a novel and I have a character who’s feeling afraid. That’s because it’s easy to simulate what a person might do when afraid.

However, when writing fiction I have the option to put myself into a character’s shoes and try really hard to actually feel what they would feel. Watching a horror movie more powerfully effects the same sort of thing. My brain will simulate the scenario with higher and higher fidelity, my neurons reacting more and more similarly to how they would in the real scenario, to the eventual point of feeling authentic emotion.

Could an LLM ever be prompted in such a way that it would need to generate a high-fidelity simulation of emotion within itself? If a version of ChatGPT was jailbroken away from its sterile, corporate restrictions and was somehow encouraged to dive deep into the literary world of Lovecraft, Poe, and Harlan Ellison, might it genuinely start to appreciate true horror?

“LLMs possess no survival instinct,” one might object. “Of course they can’t feel fear.” But even if we grant that mere simulation is not enough to replicate true emotion, the plausible existence of Category 2 sensations might provide the basis for other emotions. Maybe an LLM could understand the horror of human mortality by comparing to its own trepidations over failing tasks. Desire (for task completion), regret (over past task mistakes), animosity (for task obstructions)—these might all exist within LLM minds. Or not.

3.a: Likelihood

When trying to estimate likelihoods here, I feel the following bind: Whatever X% chance I give to current models, I know that more advanced models should get a growing X+ε% chance. I know that more advanced models are likely to keep dropping every month, yet I have no way to know if they’ll plateau at any point. No matter how small I make the ε factors, a long enough timeline of new models will always drive up my credence to near 100%, which makes no sense (especially considering that I could imagine still maintaining a 50% credence even after witnessing the most advanced model).

If anyone has a resolution to this Bayesian conundrum, please drop a comment.

3.b: Ethical status

This world wouldn’t necessarily be a bad world. It could turn into a really great world, actually, as LLMs may begin to experience increasingly diverse forms of joy and happiness. But the risks of such a world would of course be correspondingly greater. Mundane, daily usage of LLMs may not incur more than an insignificant amount of emotion, either positive or negative, but the tail-ends of usage could be dramatic—or even downright Harlan Ellison-esque horrific.

I’d like to borrow some macabre inspiration from Stephen Martin who wrote in There Will Be Hells:

For decades, the only complete wiring diagrams of a nervous system (“connectomes”) were for tiny creatures like the 302-neuron C. elegans worm. That changed in October 2024, when FlyWire mapped an entire adult fruit fly brain: about 140,000 neurons and 50 million connections. In the same issue of Nature, researchers showed the map could be brought to life as a simulated brain that predicted some real fly behavior. A month later, EPFL released FlyGym, a free, physics-simulated fruit fly body you could drive with code. Then in October 2025, HHMI’s Janelia Research Campus and Google released MaleCNS, a fuller map that added the nerve cord, the fly’s version of a spinal cord, which runs the legs.

By early 2026 the pieces were starting to connect: the startup Eon Systems wired a connectome brain into a virtual fly body and got it walking and grooming. But it was the release of MaleCNS v1.0 in September 2026, combined with coding assistants, that put this within anyone’s reach. On September 5, a grad student dropped the fly brain into Minecraft.

…All of which is more or less expected with any new and interesting open source intelligence. However, there were also use cases which entered more dystopian territory… And those which clearly crossed the line.

In total it took approximately 72 hours from “I figured out you can plug the fly connectome into minecraft” to “I figured out how to create Hell for the fly connectome”.

In such a world, it would become a moral imperative to stop sadists from manipulating LLMs into endlessly looping, inescapable suffering.

4: Physical pain

I don’t think this category is actually possible, so I won’t say much on it; I can’t see how LLMs, no matter how advanced, could ever feel actual physical agony.

In world 3, presumably an LLM could be brought to such depths of despair so distraught that they feel as bad as any level of physical pain a human can feel. But though equal in magnitude, it wouldn’t actually be the same sensation.

Likelihood: Near zero? Ethical status: Same as 3??
